newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil CVRD delay affects consortia differently.
newsitem.headline: Brazil CVRD delay affects consortia differently.

text.p: The delay in the privatization auction of Brazilian mining giant CVRD is reportedly irking one of the bidding consortia while the postponement is being seen as benefitting the other.

The auction of a 45-percent voting stake in CVRD was scheduled for April 29, but a flood of lawsuits has managed to halt the privatization process until further court action decides the validity of the legal challenges.

"The delay is not causing any major problems for the consortia. The costs involved are reasonable. They are not unsustainable," said Rodrigo Marques, analyst at Bozano Simonsen. "Theoretically, it is an advantage for CSN. It can improve the structure of its consortium."
Brazilian steelmaker CSN's Valepar consortium has been seen as weak and disorganized in comparison with its rival Valecom because of the continuous flux of members leaving and joining.

A spokesman for Valecom said CSN was benefiting from the delay in the privatization auction because it was gaining more time to recruit new members for its consortium, whereas Valecom's group was already clearly defined and firm.

But, CSN Chairman Benjamin Steinbruch has shrugged off such comments, saying the nucleus of Valepar had been formed and while new members were welcome they were not essential for the consortium's ability to place a bid.

"We consider the informality or flexibility of our consortium to be positive and we have encouraged it on purpose," Steinbruch told reporters. "It does not mean the consortium is disorganized or unstable."

Meanwhile, the chief executive of Brazil's largest private conglomerate Votorantim, Antonio Ermirio de Moraes, the leader of Valecom, reportedly expressed irritation over the auction delay, saying Brazil is putting on a "third-world show".
"The judiciary is sovereign and I shall not criticize it, but one can understand the irritation all of us are experiencing," Moraes told O Globo newspaper.
Votorantim company directors were not immediately available to confirm the text of the comments as published in O Globo.

Both consortia say they are incurring extra costs because of the delay in the sell-off relating to financial guarantees worth $3 billion which had to be deposited to qualify for the auction as well as to loans taken up to finance bids.

Valepar's principal members are NationsBank, Opportunity Asset Management and four Brazilian pension funds, but the group is still holding talks with U.S. aluminium company Alcoa, Brazil's pulp and paper group Cia. Suzano, Japanese investors and South Africa's Gencor.

Apart from Votorantim, Valecom includes South Africa's Anglo-American Corp, two pension funds, a group of 11 Japanese steelmakers and trading companies and Brazil's metal and metallurgical group Caemi, 40-percent owned by Japan's Mitsui & Co.
